## Intent
Hypothesis: Halide code generation of a branchless blend formulation with per-particle hash RNG can approach the streaming ceiling by eliminating branchy respawn overhead.

## Layout & approach
The AoS layout at 68 B/particle offers 32 hot bytes (47%) for loop 1 (age+pos+seed+vel) and 28 hot bytes (41%) for loop 2 (color+pos); over half each cacheline is dead weight dragged through the line filler. No intermediate storage keeps the death verdict in registers — no extra bandwidth. The branchless blend approach should avoid misprediction, and per-particle hash RNG avoids divergent access. With 68·N working set, L1d spills at N≈481, L2 at N≈7710, L3 at N≈246723 — all measured N are L3-resident or DRAM, so the loop always streams.

## Cache saturation
The ns/particle is flat across all N: 37.2 ns/p at N=10000 (L3) vs 36.2 ns/p at N=10000000 (DRAM) at q=0.01 — no cache-spill knee. The L3→DRAM transition at N≈246723 produces no cost increase; if anything, cost slightly decreases at larger N. This flatness signals compute/frontend dominance — per-particle overhead dwarfs memory latency at every regime. The dense grid reveals no knee because there is none.

## Bandwidth
Achieved bandwidth is 1.66–1.88 GB/s — 13–15% of the 12.69 GB/s ceiling. The memory floor of 5.359 ns/p frames irreducible memory time; the algo runs at 36–41 ns/p, ~7× the floor, confirming compute/frontend-bound, not bandwidth-bound. Profiles confirm: frontend_stall dominates at 55–60%, backend_stall=0%, branch_flush=0%. Against baseline, 1.464× faster at q=0.01 but only 1.143× at q=0.5 — respawn overhead erodes the edge. Against the autovec winner, 4.828× slower at q=0.01 narrowing to 2.113× at q=0.5 — the winner's vectorization degrades faster with death rate.

## Assembly
The codegen is entirely scalar: 0 vector-suffixed instructions. The loop processes one particle per iteration with `vmovss` loads at stride 0x44 (68 bytes), `vucomiss` comparisons, and `vmulss`/`vaddss`/`vsubss` arithmetic. Despite the "branchless blend" declaration, the code is branchy: 24 `cmp`, 10 `jae`, 6 `jne`, plus `sets`/`setge`/`cmovae` predicates. The render section does byte-granular scatter: `movzx edx, BYTE PTR [r13+r15*1+0x0]`, `add`, `cmp bx,0xff`, `cmovae`, `mov BYTE PTR` — read-modify-write per channel. The 413-instruction body with `sub rsp,0x448` and a `call halide_b2` explains the 55–60% frontend stall: the instruction footprint overflows the micro-op cache. Scalar stride-68 access explains the 1.83 GB/s achieved bandwidth.

## Verdict
Refuted — Halide produced scalar, branchy code (0 vector instructions, 24 `cmp`, 10 `jae`) rather than the branchless blend promised. It beats naive scalar everywhere (1.14–1.46×) via better register allocation, but is 2.1–4.8× slower than the autovec winner at every N×q. The 55–60% frontend stall from the 413-instruction body, combined with scalar-only `vmovss`/`vmulss`, caps bandwidth at 13–15% of ceiling. The narrowing gap at high death rates (4.828×→2.113× vs winner) reflects the winner's vectorization degrading, not this algo improving.
